subject: history

questions.content: What is the main difference between a reformer and a revolutionary?
options: A reformer seeks to change a system from within, while a revolutionary seeks to overthrow it
They mean exactly the same thing
questions.explanation: Reformers aim for gradual change within existing institutions. Revolutionaries aim for rapid, fundamental change, often by overthrowing those in power.

questions.content: For what is Florence Nightingale best remembered?
options: Improving nursing and hospital hygiene, beginning with her work in the Crimean War
questions.explanation: She nursed British soldiers in the Crimean War (1854-56) and later helped found professional nurse training.

questions.content: Which method did Mahatma Gandhi use to campaign against British rule in India?
questions.explanation: Gandhi promoted nonviolent resistance, including boycotts, marches and refusing to obey unjust laws.

questions.content: In which year did Nelson Mandela become president of South Africa?
questions.explanation: Mandela was elected in the first democratic elections in 1994 and served until 1999.

questions.content: Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union in 1903 to campaign for what?
questions.explanation: The WSPU, whose members became known as suffragettes, used more militant tactics than earlier campaigners.

questions.content: What was the aim of Gandhi's Salt March of 1930?
options: To protest the British salt tax and monopoly
To start a war with Pakistan
To ask for a new currency
questions.explanation: Gandhi and his followers marched to the sea to make salt, breaking the law, in a symbolic act of nonviolent protest.

questions.content: The Montgomery Bus Boycott of 1955-56 was a protest against what?
questions.explanation: African American residents refused to use the buses for over a year. The campaign helped to launch Martin Luther King Jr. as a national leader.

questions.content: Toussaint Louverture is remembered for his leadership in which event?
options: The revolution of enslaved people against French colonial rule in Saint-Domingue, leading to independent Haiti
questions.explanation: The Haitian Revolution led to independence in 1804, creating the first state led by formerly enslaved people.

questions.content: Nelson Mandela was imprisoned after 1962 and released in 1990. Approximately how long did he spend in prison?
questions.explanation: From 1962 to 1990 is 28 calendar years, and he was in prison for about 27 years because he was released in February 1990.

questions.content: What is the main difference between suffragists and suffragettes in Britain?
options: Suffragists used peaceful methods, while suffragettes used more militant tactics
Suffragists were against votes for women
questions.explanation: Millicent Fawcett's suffragists used petitions and lawful campaigning, while the WSPU's suffragettes broke windows and disrupted events.

questions.content: In October 1917 the Bolsheviks under Lenin did what?
options: Took power in Russia by overthrowing the Provisional Government
questions.explanation: The Bolsheviks seized control of Petrograd, and Lenin became head of the new Soviet government.

questions.content: William Wilberforce, a Member of Parliament, campaigned for the abolition of the slave trade. How is he best classified?
options: A revolutionary who overthrew the king
A reformer who worked within the political system
questions.explanation: Wilberforce worked through Parliament. Slavery was abolished across most of the British Empire by the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833.

questions.content: A student claims that Gandhi alone caused Indian independence in 1947. Which additional factor best shows the claim is too simple?
options: Britain was financially and militarily weakened by the Second World War
questions.explanation: Independence resulted from several causes, including other nationalist leaders, mass movements and British weakness after 1945.

questions.content: Which statement most accurately compares Gandhi and Mandela?
options: Both challenged unjust systems, but Mandela later supported armed sabotage after peaceful protest was met with repression
Both led armed revolutions from the start
Both held office in the same government
questions.explanation: Mandela helped found the armed wing of the ANC, Umkhonto we Sizwe, in 1961, after the Sharpeville killings of 1960. Later he negotiated an end to apartheid.

questions.content: Which argument best supports the view that Florence Nightingale was historically significant?
options: She was born into a wealthy family
She lived to an old age
Her work shaped professional nurse training and used statistics to argue for better hospital conditions, with lasting impact
questions.explanation: Significance is judged by lasting influence on many people, not by personal details.

questions.content: Some historians criticise the 'great man' approach to history. What is their main objection?
options: It uses too many primary sources
It overlooks the roles of ordinary people and wider social forces
It only studies the modern world
questions.explanation: Movements succeed because thousands of people take part. Leaders are important, but so are the groups and conditions around them.

questions.content: Robespierre was a leader during the French Revolution, including the Reign of Terror of 1793-94. What does this suggest about revolutions?
options: Revolutionary change can bring violence and repression, as well as hopes for equality
questions.explanation: The Terror saw thousands executed. Evaluations of revolutionaries should consider both their aims and their methods.

questions.content: In 1993 Nelson Mandela and F. W. de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize. What does this best suggest?
options: International recognition that ending apartheid required negotiation between both sides
That de Klerk had always opposed apartheid
That the apartheid system had already ended in 1960
That Mandela had never been in prison
questions.explanation: The award honoured their joint work in negotiating a peaceful transition to democracy. It does not imply that de Klerk's earlier role was blameless.

note:
## Reformers and revolutionaries
Historians often study individuals because their decisions and actions had a large effect on events. A **reformer** works to change a system from within, usually through laws, campaigns and persuasion. A **revolutionary** wants to overthrow the existing system, often rapidly and sometimes through violence. The line between them can blur, and some people change approach over time.

## Key individuals and what to remember
- **Elizabeth Fry**: campaigned for better conditions for prisoners in early 19th-century Britain.
- **Florence Nightingale**: nursed soldiers in the Crimean War (1854-56), then promoted hygiene, statistics and professional nurse training.
- **William Wilberforce**: an MP who led campaigns against the slave trade. The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 ended slavery across most of the British Empire.
- **Emmeline Pankhurst**: founded the Women's Social and Political Union in 1903. Suffragettes used militant tactics, whereas suffragists such as Millicent Fawcett used peaceful, lawful methods.
- **Toussaint Louverture**: leader of the Haitian Revolution of enslaved people against French colonial rule. Haiti became independent in 1804.
- **Robespierre**: a leading figure in the French Revolution, closely linked to the Reign of Terror (1793-94).
- **Lenin**: led the Bolsheviks to power in Russia in October 1917.
- **Gandhi**: used nonviolent civil disobedience, such as the Salt March of 1930, against British rule in India, which ended in 1947.
- **Martin Luther King Jr.**: leader of the civil rights movement, prominent in the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-56) and the March on Washington (1963).
- **Nelson Mandela**: opposed apartheid, was imprisoned from 1962 to 1990, shared the Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk in 1993 and became president in 1994.

## Judging significance
Ask these questions: How many people were affected? How deeply? For how long? Did the individual cause change, or were wider forces at work? For example, Gandhi's campaigns mattered, but Britain's weakness after the Second World War and other nationalist movements also help explain Indian independence in 1947.

## Interpretations
Historians disagree about individuals. Some praise leaders as heroes; others stress the role of ordinary people and wider social forces and criticise the 'great man' view of history. Evaluate interpretations by checking their evidence and purposes.

## Worked example
Question: Compare Gandhi and Mandela. Both challenged unjust systems and both spent time in prison. Gandhi stayed committed to nonviolence. Mandela began with peaceful protest, but after the Sharpeville killings of 1960 and the banning of the ANC, he helped found an armed wing in 1961. Later he negotiated a peaceful transition. A strong answer gives a similarity, a difference and a judgement.

## Common mistakes
- Describing an individual's life without explaining their impact.
- Crediting a single person for a change with many causes.
- Giving dates or details from memory without checking, which damages accuracy.

## How this is examined
You may receive a short biographical source, a speech extract described in your own words, or a portrait with a caption. Questions ask you to explain why the person was significant, compare two individuals, assess the reliability of a source about them and evaluate how far change was due to the individual.

Exam tip: Always link the person to the change they caused and then weigh it against other factors; do not just list facts about their life.

flashcards.back: A reformer changes a system from within, often through laws. A revolutionary seeks to overthrow the system, often rapidly.
Nursed soldiers in the Crimean War (1854-56) and promoted hygiene, statistics and professional nurse training.
Nonviolent civil disobedience, for example the Salt March of 1930 against the British salt tax.
Suffragists, led by Millicent Fawcett, used peaceful campaigning. Suffragettes, in the WSPU led by Emmeline Pankhurst, used militant tactics.
Law that ended slavery in most of the British Empire. William Wilberforce was a leading campaigner.
Leader in the Haitian Revolution against French colonial rule. Haiti became independent in 1804.
US civil rights leader prominent in the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-56) and the March on Washington (1963).
Anti-apartheid leader, imprisoned 1962-1990, Nobel Peace Prize 1993 with de Klerk, president of South Africa 1994-1999.
It overlooks the roles of ordinary people and wider forces that made change possible.

subject: history

questions.content: For what is Marie Curie best known?
questions.explanation: Marie Curie and her husband Pierre discovered the elements polonium and radium and she developed the study of radioactivity.

questions.content: Which substance did Alexander Fleming discover in 1928?
questions.explanation: Fleming noticed that a mould killed bacteria on a culture dish. Penicillin became a usable medicine later.

questions.content: What did the Wright brothers achieve in 1903?
options: The first crossing of the Atlantic by ship
The first powered, controlled aeroplane flights
questions.explanation: Orville and Wilbur Wright flew at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in December 1903.

questions.content: What does 'innovation' mean?
options: Introducing a new idea, method or device
questions.explanation: Innovations may be new inventions or new ways of using existing ideas.

questions.content: Edward Jenner is remembered for developing a vaccine against which disease?
questions.explanation: In 1796 Jenner showed that cowpox inoculation protected against smallpox.

questions.content: Why is Gutenberg's printing press, developed in the 15th century, historically significant?
options: It allowed books to be produced more cheaply and ideas to spread faster
It ended all wars in Europe
It created the first electricity grid
It made books impossible to copy
questions.explanation: Movable-type printing in Europe increased the supply of books and helped spread ideas widely.

questions.content: A factory took 12 hours to assemble a car before it introduced a moving assembly line and 2 hours afterwards. By what percentage did the assembly time fall (to the nearest whole number)?
questions.explanation: The fall is 10 hours. 10 / 12 = 0.833, which is about 83%.

questions.content: Why is it misleading to credit only Fleming for penicillin as a medicine?
options: Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their team developed it into a usable drug, and all three shared a Nobel Prize in 1945
questions.explanation: Innovations often involve teams. Fleming made the discovery in 1928 and later researchers turned it into a medicine.

questions.content: Alan Turing is remembered for which work during the Second World War?
options: Leading the Allied invasion of Normandy
Codebreaking at Bletchley Park, helping to read German encrypted messages
Building the first nuclear reactor in Britain
questions.explanation: Turing worked at Bletchley Park. He had also described the idea of a general-purpose computing machine in 1936.

questions.content: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images of DNA were important because they did what?
options: They provided evidence that helped Watson and Crick work out the double-helix structure in 1953
They proved DNA does not exist
They were used to build aeroplanes
questions.explanation: Franklin's work was key to understanding DNA, but her contribution was not widely recognised at the time.

questions.content: Which statement about the World Wide Web is correct?
options: It is identical to the internet
It was developed by the Wright brothers
It is a system for sharing information using hyperlinks over the internet, developed by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN
questions.explanation: The internet is the underlying network. The Web is a service that runs on it. Berners-Lee developed it around 1989-1991.

questions.content: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in Physics (1903, shared) and Chemistry (1911). Why is this unusual?
options: She won them in the same year
She won in two different sciences, which was a very rare achievement
questions.explanation: Her two prizes in different scientific fields made her a famous pioneer, and she was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

questions.content: Which measure best shows that an innovation is historically significant?
options: The cost of its first model
The number of people affected and how long the effects lasted
How famous its inventor was at birth
questions.explanation: Historians judge significance by breadth, depth and duration of impact.

questions.content: Thomas Edison is often called the inventor of the light bulb. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Several inventors, such as Joseph Swan, developed electric lamps, and Edison improved a practical bulb and a supply system
No one else worked on electric lights
questions.explanation: Many inventions are the result of several people's work. Historians weigh who improved, developed and popularised them.

questions.content: Why did penicillin move from laboratory discovery to mass production in the 1940s?
options: It was easily made at home
The Second World War created high demand for medicine to treat wounded soldiers, and governments supported production
questions.explanation: Context matters: wartime need and funding helped turn discovery into large-scale manufacturing.

questions.content: Henry Ford's assembly line made cars cheaper, but some critics said it made factory work repetitive. What does this show about innovation?
options: Innovations can bring benefits for some groups and costs for others
questions.explanation: Evaluation requires considering several groups and both positive and negative effects.

questions.content: A biography of a famous pioneer was written by a member of their family. What is the main limitation?
options: Family members never know the subject
The author may emphasise achievements and leave out faults
questions.explanation: Close relationships can affect balance. The author's origin and purpose should be checked, and other sources used.

questions.content: Tu Youyou received the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on a malaria treatment, and her research drew on traditional Chinese medicine texts. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Modern science can build on older knowledge traditions
questions.explanation: Innovation can combine new methods with earlier knowledge. It does not mean that all traditional remedies work.

note:
## Pioneers and innovators
A **pioneer** is the first to explore or develop something new. An **innovation** is the introduction of a new idea, method or device. Historians study pioneers to understand how knowledge and technology change society, but they also ask who else contributed and who benefited.

## Key individuals and what to remember
- **Johannes Gutenberg**: developed movable-type printing in Europe in the 15th century, making books cheaper and helping ideas spread.
- **Edward Jenner**: in 1796 showed that cowpox inoculation protected against smallpox, an early step towards vaccination.
- **Marie Curie**: pioneered research on radioactivity, discovered polonium and radium and won Nobel Prizes in Physics (1903, shared) and Chemistry (1911).
- **Wright brothers**: made the first powered, controlled aeroplane flights in December 1903 at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
- **Alexander Fleming**: discovered penicillin in 1928. Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their team developed it into a medicine in the 1940s, and all three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.
- **Rosalind Franklin**: her X-ray images of DNA helped Watson and Crick work out the double helix in 1953.
- **Alan Turing**: codebreaker at Bletchley Park in the Second World War and an early thinker about general-purpose computing.
- **Tim Berners-Lee**: developed the World Wide Web at CERN around 1989-1991. The Web is a service that runs on the internet, not the same thing.
- **Tu Youyou**: won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on a malaria treatment, using traditional Chinese medicine texts as one source of ideas.

## Judging significance
Ask: How many people were affected? How deeply? For how long? Did the innovation change daily life, health, work or communication? Also look at limitations and costs. Henry Ford's moving assembly line cut production times and made cars cheaper, but critics said it made work repetitive.

## Credit and teamwork
Historians are cautious about crediting a single person. Many inventions involve teams, earlier ideas and the right context. Thomas Edison improved the practical electric light bulb, but other inventors, such as Joseph Swan, also developed electric lamps. Penicillin became a mass-produced medicine in the 1940s partly because wartime needs created demand.

## Worked example
Before its moving line, a factory took 12 hours to assemble one car. After, it took 2 hours. Fall in time = 12 - 2 = 10 hours. Percentage fall = 10 / 12 x 100 = 83.3%, about 83%. A good evaluation then asks: who gained (customers, owners) and who may have lost (workers whose jobs became repetitive)?

## Common mistakes
- Saying 'X invented Y' when many people contributed.
- Describing what the innovation was but not its effect.
- Forgetting negative effects or groups who did not benefit.
- Confusing the internet with the World Wide Web.

## How this is examined
Questions might give a short source about a discovery and ask what it shows about the process of innovation, who deserves credit, and how far it changed life. Extended tasks ask you to evaluate the significance of an innovation using criteria such as reach, depth and duration, and to consider different perspectives.

Exam tip: Support every claim of significance with evidence about who was affected and for how long; avoid claiming that one person worked alone.

flashcards.back: Introducing a new idea, method or device.
Developed smallpox vaccination in 1796 using cowpox.
Pioneer of radioactivity research. Discovered polonium and radium. Nobel Prizes in Physics (1903, shared) and Chemistry (1911).
Made the first powered, controlled aeroplane flights in December 1903 at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
Discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928. Developed into a medicine by Florey, Chain and their team in the 1940s.
Her X-ray images of DNA helped Watson and Crick work out the double-helix structure in 1953.
Codebreaker at Bletchley Park in the Second World War and early thinker on general-purpose computing.
Information system using hyperlinks that runs on the internet. Developed by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN around 1989-1991.
Consider how many people were affected, how deeply, for how long, and for whom there were benefits and costs.
